Battle of Thermopylae. At the narrow coastal pass of Thermopylae in central Greece, in 480 BC, Spartan King Leonidas I led a Greek coalition in a legendary stand against the invading Persian army of Xerxes I. Though they were ultimately defeated, the Greeks' dogged defense inflicted heavy Persian casualties and bought precious time for other city-states to organize their resistance.

Leonidas commanded roughly 7,000 Greek hoplites, with approximately 300 Spartans forming the core of his force. Xerxes I commanded an enormous Persian force. Ancient sources claim over 100,000 soldiers, though historians debate whether the true number was somewhat smaller.

The narrow terrain at Thermopylae neutralized the Persians' numerical advantage. The Greek phalanx discipline allowed the hoplites to dominate in the confined space. For three days, fierce combat raged at the pass, with the Greeks holding firm against repeated Persian assaults.

But Thermopylae's defenders could not hold forever. A traitor revealed a mountain path that allowed the Persians to outflank the Greek position. Facing encirclement, most of the Greek force withdrew to fight another day. But Leonidas and the Spartans made a different choice. Rather than retreat, they chose to stand and die, covering the Greek withdrawal with their lives.

Leonidas and roughly 1,100 Greeks perished in this final stand. Persian losses reportedly reached 20,000. The Spartans had become legends. Leonidas himself became the iconic symbol of Spartan valor and sacrifice, embodying the warrior culture that produced him. Xerxes had invaded Greece with seemingly infinite power, yet his force had been stopped at this narrow pass. The battle set the stage for later victories at Salamis, where Athenian naval forces would avenge Thermopylae.
